primary_meaning: God's forensic (legal) declaration that a sinner is righteous and in right standing with Him, based on faith in Christ's atoning work rather than personal merit or works of the law; often involving the imputation of Christ's righteousness

alternatives.meaning: A transformative process in which God both declares and actually makes the person righteous by infused grace, involving cooperation with the Spirit, sacraments, and good works (not merely forensic imputation)
basis: Catholic catechetical tradition on justification as progressive sanctification

alternatives.meaning: Covenant membership and eschatological vindication of God's people (New Perspective on Paul and related readings): justification primarily concerns inclusion in Abraham's family and status as God's people rather than individual forensic acquittal from sin guilt
basis: works of N.T. Wright, E.P. Sanders, James Dunn

alternatives.meaning: Old Testament background sense of judicial vindication, righting of wrongs, or demonstration of covenant faithfulness (less focused on individual soteriology)

notes: Justification is a core soteriological doctrine employing forensic/legal metaphor rather than pure symbolism; the Reformation forensic reading remains the most widely taught primary sense in evangelical and classical Protestant instruction and much biblical commentary, yet major denominational and scholarly alternatives prevent a single settled consensus across all Christian traditions and academic biblical studies.
